proposals.before: Tai was at first an erudite of the Imperial Academy and a staff officer in the two offices of General-in-Chief Xie An and Rapid Cavalry General the Prince of Kuaiji, Daozi.
proposals.after: Tai was at first an erudite of the Imperial Academy and a staff officer in the two offices of Guard General Xie An and Rapid Cavalry General the Prince of Kuaiji, Daozi.

proposals.after: His grandfather, Wang, had served as Jin's General Who Pacifies the North and as inspector of Xu and Yan provinces.

proposals.before: Yang Xiong drafted the Profound Meaning while still very young;
proposals.after: Yang Wu took part in the Profound Meaning while still very young;

proposals.after: Biographies 20: Fan Tai, Wang Zhunzhi, Wang Shaozhi, and Xun Bozi

proposals.before: Thus Yu of Xia took upon himself the people's faults, Tang of Yin willingly bore the myriad regions' errors, Tai Jia used the mulberry-and-grain omen to advance in virtue, and King Jing of Song used the Mars omen to cultivate goodness—all turned misfortune into success, as past events make clear.
proposals.after: Thus Yu of Xia took upon himself the people's faults, Tang of Yin willingly bore the myriad regions' errors, Tai Wu used the mulberry-and-grain omen to advance in virtue, and King Jing of Song used the Mars omen to cultivate goodness—all turned misfortune into success, as past events make clear.
proposals.reason: Chinese 太戊 is Shang king Tai Wu, not Tai Jia (太甲); the mulberry-and-grain omen belongs to Tai Wu.

proposals.before: Thus Yu of Xia cited the crimes of the hundred surnames, Tang of Yin willingly bore the faults of the myriad regions, Tai Jia relied on mulberry and grain to advance in virtue, and King Jing of Song borrowed the Mars intrusion to cultivate goodness—these all turned defeat into success, as past affairs make clear.
proposals.after: Thus Yu of Xia cited the crimes of the hundred surnames, Tang of Yin willingly bore the faults of the myriad regions, Tai Wu relied on mulberry and grain to advance in virtue, and King Jing of Song borrowed the Mars intrusion to cultivate goodness—these all turned defeat into success, as past affairs make clear.
proposals.reason: Literal English likewise renders 太戊 as Tai Jia; the source name is Tai Wu.

proposals.before: The responsible office memorialized to impeach him; the Founding Emperor took no notice.
proposals.after: The responsible office memorialized to impeach him; Taizu took no notice.
proposals.reason: 太祖 in this Songshu biography is Emperor Wen, not the founding emperor (高祖).

proposals.before: The responsible office memorialized to impeach him; the Founding Emperor did not inquire.
proposals.after: The responsible office memorialized to impeach him; Taizu did not inquire.
proposals.reason: Literal English also renders 太祖 as Founding Emperor, which misidentifies Emperor Wen.

proposals.before: At that time though the Founding Emperor personally held the reins of government, Xianzhi and others still held heavy power; he again submitted a memorial, saying: 'Your servant has heard that the Prince of Luling has already had his title and fief restored, yet posthumous honors have not been added.

proposals.before: My slight aim does not hope to witness the flourishing transformation with my own eyes; I secretly admire Zisang's heart in defending Ying and hope to avoid Xun Yan's regret of dying with eyes open.
proposals.after: My slight aim does not hope to witness the flourishing transformation with my own eyes; I secretly admire Zi Nang's heart in walling Ying and hope to avoid Xun Yan's regret of dying with eyes open.
proposals.reason: 子囊 is the Chu minister Zi Nang, not Zisang; 城郢 is walling/fortifying Ying.

proposals.before: Great Song, though it received the throne by yielding, has not yet accumulated the Way of Yu and Shun; the day the former emperor died was the beginning of the Way's decline.
proposals.after: Great Song, though it received the throne by yielding, has not yet accumulated the Way of Youyu (Shun); the day the former emperor died was the beginning of the Way's decline.
proposals.reason: 有虞之道 is the Way of Youyu/Shun; the English adds Yu, who is not named in this sentence.

proposals.before: The youngest son Guangyuan was skilled at prose composition; he was an advising staff officer to the Founding Emperor's son the General Who Pacifies the Army and headed the secretariat; because of Ye's affair he was executed with him.
proposals.after: The youngest son Guangyuan was skilled at prose composition; he was an advising staff officer to Shizu, the General Who Pacifies the Army, and headed the secretariat; because of Ye's affair he was executed with him.
proposals.reason: 世祖 is the temple name Shizu, not the Founding Emperor, and the English invents Founding Emperor's son.

proposals.before: The youngest son Guangyuan was skilled at composing prose; he was Adviser Staff Officer to the Founding Emperor's son the General Who Pacifies the Army and headed the secretariat office; because of Ye's affair he was executed with him.
proposals.after: The youngest son Guangyuan was skilled at composing prose; he was Adviser Staff Officer to Shizu as General Who Pacifies the Army and headed the secretariat office; because of Ye's affair he was executed with him.
proposals.reason: Literal English likewise misreads 世祖 as Founding Emperor and inserts a son not present in the Chinese.

proposals.before: His grandfather Linzhi, father Nazhi, and all were Censors-in-Chief.
proposals.after: His grandfather Linzhi and father Nazhi had both been Censors-in-Chief.
proposals.reason: 並 means both men held the post; and all were invents extra subjects.

proposals.before: Posthumously he was enfeoffed as grand master of splendid happiness.
proposals.after: Posthumously he was granted the office of grand minister of ceremonies.
proposals.reason: 追贈太常 is a posthumous grant of the Taichang (minister of ceremonies), not an enfeoffment as 光祿大夫 (grand master of splendid happiness).

proposals.before: Posthumously he was enfeoffed as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
proposals.after: Posthumously he was granted Grand Minister of Ceremonies.

proposals.before: While compiling Jin history, Shaozhi recorded Wang Xun's profiteering and Wang Mi's rebellion.
proposals.after: While compiling Jin history, Shaozhi recorded Wang Xun's profiteering and Wang Xin's rebellion.
proposals.reason: 王廞 is conventionally Xin, not Mi; the English given name does not match the Chinese.

proposals.before: In compiling Jin history, Shaozhi recorded Wang Xun's profiteering and Wang Mi's rebellion.
proposals.after: In compiling Jin history, Shaozhi recorded Wang Xun's profiteering and Wang Xin's rebellion.
proposals.reason: 王廞 should be romanized Xin rather than Mi.

proposals.before: The late Grand Tutor, Marquis Juping Huo, combined bright virtue with penetrating worth and stood second to none among the imperial clans; his merit joined in assisting the Mandate, and when the work of pacifying Wu was done, still his later line was cut off and no one offered the seasonal sacrifices.
proposals.after: The late Grand Tutor, Marquis Juping Hu, combined bright virtue with penetrating worth and stood second to none among the eminent ministers; his merit joined in assisting the Mandate, and when the work of pacifying Wu was done, still his later line was cut off and no one offered the seasonal sacrifices.
proposals.reason: 祜 is Hu, not Huo; 宗臣 means eminent ministers, not imperial clans.

proposals.before: The former supernumerary palace attendant, Duke of Jiangxia Wei Yun, submitted a memorial in his own name, saying, "My founding ancestor, the late Grand Guardian Guan, in the middle of the Wei period of Xianxi, when the founding Emperor Wen was chief minister, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiaoyang;

proposals.reason: 衛璵 is Yu, not Yun.

proposals.before: At that time the commoner Jia and the various princes held power; jealous of Guan's loyal integrity, Prince Yun of Chu forged an edict and brought disaster upon him.
proposals.after: At that time the commoner Jia and the various princes held power; jealous of Guan's loyal integrity, Prince Wei of Chu forged an edict and brought disaster upon him.

decisions.reason: s0005 names Xie An 衛將軍, Guard General, not 大將軍 / General-in-Chief; the rest of the sentence is accurate.
The literal field makes the same title error: 衛將軍 is Guard General, not General-in-Chief.
祖汪 is the grandfather's given name, already rendered on the same pattern as 父寧 / His father Ning. Inserting commas is stylistic and does not distinguish given name from the surname Wang.
The subject is 揚烏, Yang Wu, and 豫《玄》 means he took part in the Profound Meaning, not that Yang Xiong drafted it.
Literal English likewise substitutes Yang Xiong and 'composed' for 揚烏豫《玄》; Yang Wu took part while still in tender years.
The heading person is the ritualist 王准之 (courtesy name 元曾). 淮 is a common graphic variant of 准/準, and Huaizhi misreads the name; CText's Songshu contents list 王准之.
